Account drawn from the grounding books and verified against the National Park Service and HISTORY timelines: occupation began November 20, 1969; the island was a former federal prison closed in 1963; the occupation ended June 11, 1971.
stimulus.text:
The photograph shows a wall on Alcatraz Island painted with the words "WELCOME" and "INDIAN LAND." A sign on the wall reads "UNITED INDIAN PROPERTY."

On November 20, 1969, a group of activists calling themselves Indians of All Tribes landed on Alcatraz Island, a former federal prison in San Francisco Bay that the government had closed in 1963. They claimed the island by right of discovery and said they would build an Indian school, cultural center, and museum there. The occupation lasted until June 1971.

rationales.A: The passage describes an occupation, not a lawsuit.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about foreign governments.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Like the sit-ins and Freedom Rides of the early 1960s, the Alcatraz occupation used direct action to put an injustice before the public.
rationales.D: The occupation lasted about nineteen months and did not win the island.
rationales.general:
1. The occupiers landed on the island and stayed, putting their bodies where the public could see them.
2. Background: That is direct action, the same kind of tactic as the sit-ins and Freedom Rides of the early 1960s.
3. In both cases the point was to force the country to notice an injustice it had ignored.
4. The tactic differs from a lawsuit or a lobbying campaign, which works out of public view.
Remember: Different movements can share a tactic even when their goals are different.
